facts.statement: Volia lived during the Pleistocene and possibly the Holocene.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Pleistocene - Holocene?

facts.statement: The genus Volia was described by Molnar, Worthy, and Willis in 2002.
facts.quote: authority: Molnar, Worthy & Willis, 2002

facts.statement: The type species of Volia is Volia athollandersoni.
facts.quote: type_species: Volia athollandersoni

facts.statement: Volia is an extinct genus containing only one species and is a mekosuchine crocodylian related to Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus.
facts.quote: Volia is an extinct monospecific genus of mekosuchine crocodylian closely related to Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus.

facts.statement: Fossils of Volia have been found in caves on Viti Levu and the island of Naigani in Fiji.
facts.quote: Volia is known from a collection of largely fragmentary remains including skull bones and limbs recovered from the Voli Voli and Wainibuku Caves on Viti Levu (Fiji), with similar remains having been found on Naigani.

facts.statement: Volia was approximately 2 to 3 meters long, making it the largest predator and likely apex predator of Pleistocene Fiji.
facts.quote: It was around 2 – 3 m long, making it the largest predatory animal on the island and subsequently most likely the apex predator of the Pleistocene ecosystems of Fiji.

facts.statement: Volia likely fed on giant iguanas, flightless birds, or fish.
facts.quote: It may have fed on giant iguanas, flightless birds or even fish.

facts.statement: Volia may have been more terrestrial than modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: Like its closest relatives, it may have been more terrestrial than today's crocodiles.

facts.statement: Fossils of Volia were discovered by Trevor Worthy and Atholl Anderson in 1997 and 1998.
facts.quote: The remains were uncovered when paleontologist Trevor Worthy and archaeologist Atholl Anderson searched Viti Levu for potential fossil deposits in 1997 and 1998

facts.statement: The holotype of Volia was found in Wainibuku Cave, while the largest fossils came from Voli Voli Cave.
facts.quote: The holotype was recovered from the Wainibuku Cave, but the Voli Voli Cave yielded the first and largest fossils.

facts.statement: The holotype of Volia is housed at the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa.
facts.quote: The holotype is housed in the collection of the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa.

facts.statement: Additional fossils, including an osteoderm, tooth, and skull fragment, were found on the island of Naigani.
facts.quote: Later research also discovered an additional osteoderm, tooth and a skull fragment on the island of Naigani

facts.statement: The genus name Volia comes from Voli Voli Cave, and the species name honors archaeologist Atholl Anderson.
facts.quote: The name Volia is derived from the Voli Voli Cave, while the species was named after the New Zealand archaeologist Atholl Anderson.

facts.statement: Volia had a snout proportionally deeper than a modern saltwater crocodile that ended abruptly at the tip.
facts.quote: The snout was proportionally deeper than that of today's saltwater crocodile and appears to have ended abruptly at the tip of the rostrum.

facts.statement: Volia had strongly raised eye sockets with a prominent bridge between them formed by the frontal bone.
facts.quote: The rim of the eye sockets is strongly raised by the frontal bone, which forms a prominent through between the eyes.

facts.statement: Volia had a notably shallower lower jaw compared to the related genus Mekosuchus.
facts.quote: The lower jaw of Volia is notably shallower than in the closely related species of the genus Mekosuchus

facts.statement: Volia possessed large conical teeth with oval bases that became D-shaped at the top due to asymmetrical cutting edges called carinae.
facts.quote: These include large conical teeth that are flexed somewhat inward, with an oval crosssection at their base that grows gradually more D-shaped towards the top of the crown due to the asymmetrical cutting edges, so called carinae.

facts.statement: The ridges on Volia's teeth gave them a serrated appearance, but they were not truly ziphodont like those of Quinkana.
facts.quote: While said ridges give the teeth a serrated appearance, they are not truly ziphodont like in Quinkana.

facts.statement: Thirty-five recovered osteoderms of Volia can be classified into five different morphotypes.
facts.quote: The 35 recovered osteoderms can generally be assigned to one of five different morphotypes.

facts.statement: Volia's osteoderms likely formed armor for the neck and torso, resembling those of modern spectacled caimans and saltwater crocodiles.
facts.quote: They have been compared to those of the modern spectacled caiman and saltwater crocodile, indicating that they likely formed the armor of the neck and torso.

facts.statement: One type of Volia osteoderm was oval with a prominent keel and likely covered the neck behind the occiput.
facts.quote: The third type is more distinct from these two, being oval in shape with a prominent keel running down its length. These are thought to have covered the neck, possibly being located just behind the occiput.

facts.statement: Volia's ulnare bone had a unique shape that may have allowed for hinge-like joint motion, with important biological implications.
facts.quote: Especially the last of these stands out, as it puts the joints closer together and may allow for a more hinge-like joint motion, something thought to have important implications for the animals biology.

facts.statement: Researchers estimated Volia's size by comparing its preserved femur to that of a saltwater crocodile.
facts.quote: Molnar, Worthy and Willis attempted to determine the size of one particular individual by comparing a preserved femur with the same bone in a saltwater crocodile.

facts.statement: Based on femur comparisons, Volia may have reached a length of 2 to 3 meters.
facts.quote: Assuming that the two animals shared similar proportions, this would indicate that Volia may have reached a length between 2-3 m.

facts.statement: Volia belongs to the crocodile family Crocodylidae.
facts.quote: familia: Crocodylidae

facts.statement: Volia is classified within the subfamily Mekosuchinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Mekosuchinae

facts.statement: Volia grew to be between 2 and 3 meters in length.
facts.quote: Medía entre 2 a 3 metros de largo.

facts.statement: Despite its small size, Volia was likely the largest predator in the Pleistocene ecosystems of Fiji.
facts.quote: A pesar de su pequeño tamaño, debe de haber sido el mayor depredador en los ecosistemas pleistocénicos de Fiyi.

facts.statement: Fossils of Volia athollandersoni have been found in the Voli-Voli and Wainibuku caves in the Fiji Islands.
facts.quote: Fósiles de Volia athollandersoni han sido hallados en las Islas Fiyi en las cavernas Voli-Voli y Wainibuku.

facts.statement: The holotype of Volia athollandersoni is housed in the collection of the New Zealand Museum Te Papa Tongarewa.
facts.quote: El holotipo de Volia athollandersoni se encuentra en la colección del Museo de Nueva Zelanda Te Papa Tongarewa.

facts.statement: Volia lived from the Late Pliocene to the Late Pleistocene.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Plioceno Superior - Pleistoceno Superior

facts.statement: Volia went extinct around 1000 BC.
facts.quote: extinct: 1000 a.C.

facts.statement: Volia lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Late Pleistocene to Holocene (0.129 to 0 million years ago)

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Volia may have been a terrestrial animal, similar to its relative Mekosuchus.
facts.quote: It is possible that Volia, like the closely related Mekosuchus, was a terrestrial animal.

facts.statement: The hinge-like joint motion of the distal ulnare suggests Volia was better adapted to move on land than modern saltwater crocodiles.
facts.quote: Evidence for this may be found in the anatomy of the distal ulnare, where a more hinge-like joint motion was possible, indicating it was better adapted at moving on land relative to the modern saltwater crocodile it was compared with.

facts.statement: It is speculated that Volia preyed on iguanas, large birds, or fish during the Pleistocene and possibly Holocene.
facts.quote: It is subsequently speculated that this niche could have been filled by Volia during the Pleistocene and possibly Holocene, preying on iguanas (like Lapitiguana), large birds (like Megavitiornis altirostris) or possibly fish.

facts.statement: Fossil material tentatively assigned to Volia from Naigani dates to the Holocene, around 2,900 to 2,700 years ago.
facts.quote: The material from Naigani, only tentatively assigned to Volia, also dates to the Holocene, having been recovered from an archaeological site that dates to around 2,900 to 2,700 years ago.

facts.statement: It is debated whether humans caused the extinction of Volia, as remains found in Lapita culture ovens could also belong to modern saltwater crocodiles.
facts.quote: The Naigani material was in fact found as oven contents at a Lapita culture site, however given these remains could also belong to a modern saltwater crocodile the role that humans might have played in the extinction of Volia remains uncertain.

facts.statement: Early phylogenetic studies suggested Volia was the sister taxon to Mekosuchus, with Trilophosuchus being more basal and Quinkana in a polytomy.
facts.quote: In the description of Kalthifrons by Yates and Pledge, Volia was recovered as the sister taxon to Mekosuchus, with Trilophosuchus being slightly more basal and Quinkana being part of a large polytomy due to the poor resolution of basal mekosuchines.

facts.statement: A 2023 study again identified Volia and Mekosuchus as sister taxa that were more derived than Trilophosuchus.
facts.quote: In an even more recent publication from 2023, Volia and Mekosuchus were once again found as sister taxa and more derived than Trilophosuchus.

rejected.quote: The pointed, slender front teeth and blunt, laterally compressed back teeth could have been used to crush the bones of birds and frogs alike.
